c.tagline: Where Indian Ocean trade meets colonial market streets.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rare and rarely used; always agree the fare with the driver before departing. Airport and hotel taxis typically quote fixed rates by destination.

emergency.note: Fire brigade: 995. English and French are both understood by dispatchers.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Roche Bois on the northern edge has a rough reputation and no visitor sights.
Pickpocketing around the Central Market and bus stations; the centre empties after dark, so take a taxi at night.

hood_desc: The historic harbor quarter around Caudan Waterfront and Port Louis Marina — malls, casino, museums and Champ de Mars racecourse within walking distance; the most convenient base for exploring the capital itself.

Mauritius's liveliest resort town on the north coast, about 20 minutes from the capital, packed with beach bars, restaurants and water-sports operators; suits nightlife-seekers and first-timers who want a beach base near Port Louis.

A quieter, more budget-friendly beach village just north of Grand Baie with a laid-back local feel and public beach; good for backpackers, families and travelers who want sand without the resort crowds.
A northwest coastal stretch of fishing villages and resorts between Port Louis and Pointe aux Piments; suits travelers who want all-inclusive comfort a short drive from the capital and its harbor.

Mauritius's modern business and retail hub south of the capital, home to Ebène Cybercity and Bagatelle Mall of Mauritius; best for business travelers and anyone wanting easy motorway access across the island.

water.note: Treated to WHO standards in urban areas, but quality varies; bottled water is safer, especially after heavy rain.

transit.pay: Fares are paid with the rechargeable contactless 'MyMetro' or 'M Card' smart card usable on Metro Express and most buses, or with cash directly on buses. Cards can be bought and topped up at Metro Express stations, some shops, and via the myt.mu app.
transit.hours: Metro Express runs roughly 5:30am-9:30pm; buses operate approximately 5:30am-8:30pm with sparse service after dark, so taxis fill the gap at night.
transit.note: Port Louis's core sights (waterfront, markets, Champ de Mars) are walkable; the Immigration Square terminal links the capital by Metro Express to Rose Hill, Quatre Bornes and Curepipe on the central plateau.

train: Metro Express (light rail/tram, not a national railway)
ferry: Mauritius Shipping Corporation inter-island ferry to Rodrigues, departing Port Louis harbour

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to Port Louis (~75-90 min)
Public NTC bus via Curepipe/Rose Hill (slow, transfers needed)

tip.r: Tipping is not obligatory; many restaurants add a 10% service charge already. Rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated; hotel porters and drivers welcome small tips.

food.name: Dholl puri
food.desc: Mauritius's national street food: two soft turmeric flatbreads stuffed with ground yellow split peas, rolled around bean curry, chutney and chilli.

places.name: Central Market food stalls
places.note: Upstairs and street-side counters at the Bazaar sell them hot from mid-morning.

places.name: Maraz
places.note: Near the florists; a stall regulars name when asked where to send a visitor.

places.name: Dewa and Sons
places.note: Island-famous dholl puri name with long lunchtime queues.

food.name: Mine frite
food.desc: Sino-Mauritian wok-fried egg noodles with cabbage, spring onion and soy, finished with chilli sauce and often a fried egg on top.

places.name: Chinatown stalls on Royal Road
places.note: Cluster of woks around Rue Royale turning out noodles all day.

places.name: First Restaurant
places.note: Old-school sit-down Chinatown dining room for a plated version.

places.name: Rue La Corderie lunch carts
places.note: Office-worker carts that appear at midday and sell out fast.

food.name: Gateaux piments
food.desc: Fiery little split-pea and chilli fritters, eaten by the paper cone or squashed into a bread roll with butter and chutney as a breakfast sandwich.

places.name: Central Market snack counters
places.note: Fried in batches through the morning; ask for one in a pain maison.

places.name: Desforges Street carts
places.note: Classic commuter snack strip between the market and the waterfront.

places.name: Caudan Waterfront food court
places.note: Tidier, seated option if you want the fritters without the crowd.

food.name: Rougaille
food.desc: The Creole house sauce: tomato, onion, garlic, thyme and chilli simmered with sausage, fish or chicken, served over rice with dal and pickles.

places.name: Le Courtyard
places.note: Courtyard restaurant in the old town doing proper Creole plates at lunch.

places.name: Central Market upstairs eateries
places.note: Cheap daily plate lunches of rougaille with rice and lentils.

places.name: Caudan Waterfront restaurants
places.note: Several waterfront kitchens keep a Creole rougaille on the menu.

food.name: Briani
food.desc: Mauritian biryani: layered saffron rice with marinated meat, potatoes and fried onion, steamed sealed and served with a cooling cucumber salad.

places.name: Central Market food hall
places.note: Big pots of briani sold by the plate, especially at lunchtime.

places.name: Le Courtyard
places.note: Sit-down briani in the historic core near the Government House.

places.name: Chinatown and Royal Road eateries
places.note: Small Muslim-run kitchens around the mosque area are the local pick.

food.name: Boulettes
food.desc: Steamed dumplings - chayote, fish, chicken or tofu - dropped into a clear ginger broth and eaten with chilli paste and soy.

places.name: Chinatown boulette stalls
places.note: Bamboo steamers stacked at street level near Jummah Mosque.

places.name: First Restaurant
places.note: Long-established dining room serving the full boulette assortment.

places.name: Central Market counters
places.note: Quick bowl between shopping the spice and vegetable halls.

food.name: Alouda
food.desc: Sweet chilled milk drink with basil seeds, agar jelly and vanilla or almond syrup - the drink you pair with a market lunch.

places.name: Pillay alouda stall
places.note: The market's best-known alouda counter, working since the old bazaar days.

places.name: Central Market drink stands
places.note: Several stands mix it to order; ask for less syrup if you want it lighter.

places.name: Caudan Waterfront kiosks
places.note: Easy air-conditioned alternative near the shops.

food.name: Phoenix beer and island rum
food.desc: Phoenix lager is the local staple; agricole-style rums from Mauritian distilleries turn up neat, spiced or in a rum punch.

places.name: Keg and Marlin
places.note: Waterfront pub pouring cold Phoenix with a harbour view.

places.name: Caudan Waterfront bars
places.note: Cluster of bars for rum tasting flights after dark.

places.name: Le Courtyard
places.note: Good spot for a rum punch alongside a Creole lunch.

landmarks: Aapravasi Ghat
This UNESCO World Heritage site preserves the immigration depot where indentured laborers first arrived in Mauritius, offering a poignant window into the island's history.
Caudan Waterfront
A vibrant harborside promenade lined with shops, cafes, and colorful hanging umbrellas, this lively hub blends leisure, dining, and scenic ocean views.
Champ de Mars Racecourse
The oldest horse racing track in the Southern Hemisphere, this historic grandstand-lined course has hosted thrilling races and social gatherings since 1812.
Fort Adelaide (The Citadel)
Perched on a hill above the capital, this 19th-century British fortress offers sweeping panoramic views over Port Louis, the harbor, and surrounding mountains.
Jummah Mosque
An elegant blend of Indian, Creole, and Islamic architectural styles, this 19th-century mosque with ornate archways is one of the city's most beautiful landmarks.
Port Louis Central Market
A bustling multi-level bazaar overflowing with tropical fruit, spices, textiles, and street food, capturing the colorful multicultural energy of Mauritian daily life.
Place d'Armes
A grand palm-lined boulevard leading from Government House to the harbor, this ceremonial avenue is steeped in colonial history and civic pageantry.
Government House
This handsome colonial-era building, seat of Mauritian government since French rule, showcases graceful verandas and manicured gardens in the city center.
Natural History Museum
Home to a rare stuffed dodo specimen and displays on Mauritian wildlife, this small but treasured museum offers insight into the island's unique lost species.
Chinatown
A compact historic quarter of red lanterns and traditional shopfronts reflecting Port Louis's Sino-Mauritian heritage, alive with dumpling stalls and lunar new year festivities.

train.note: Mauritius has no long-distance railway. The Metro Express serving Port Louis is an urban light-rail/tram line only. Travel around the island by bus, and reach Rodrigues Island by ferry or air.

bus.note: Island nation with no international coach routes. The main long-distance domestic operator is the state National Transport Corporation (CNT/NTC); private and regional companies also cover the island.

ferry.note: From Port Louis, Mauritius Shipping Corporation's MV Mauritius Trochetia sails to Rodrigues Island (domestic, roughly 24-36h, book well ahead) and occasionally to Agalega. There is no regular scheduled passenger ferry to Reunion - travel there by air; check the operator at mauritiusshipping.net for any sailings.
